source1: Alasdair J. M. Watson, Religious acculturation and assimilation in Belgic Gaul and Aquitania from the Roman Conquest until the end of the Second Century CE, PhD thesis, University of Edinburgh, 2005 - https://era.ed.ac.uk/handle/1842/30894
notes: Gauls practised Celtic polytheism (database 'Roman' reflects post-conquest outcome). Gallic deities persisted provincially under Roman names (Watson), but the Roman court kept Roman religion; Epona reached Rome only in imperial times via guard units.

Chandragupta's faith at conquest undocumented: Brahman adviser Kautilya, yet Digambara tradition makes him a Jain monk later. Earliest securely dated Mauryan script is Ashokan Brahmi, 3rd c. BCE (Britannica 'Brahmi'), so writing c. 321 BCE uncertain.

source2: Richard M. Eaton, The Rise of Islam and the Bengal Frontier, 1204-1760, University of California Press, 1993 - https://publishing.cdlib.org/ucpressebooks/view?docId=ft067n99v9&brand=ucpress
notes: Sur Afghans, Muslims, took Bengal 1538-39 (Britannica: early 1539) and remained Muslim, with a bureaucratic revenue system; no adoption of Hinduism. Eaton: Bengal's Muslim majority emerged later under the Mughals, so Hindu majority in 1538 plausible.

source1: Shaye J. D. Cohen, 'Roman Domination: The Jewish Revolt and the Destruction of the Second Temple', in H. Shanks (ed.), Ancient Israel, Biblical Archaeology Society, 1999 - https://cojs.org/shaye_cohen-_-roman_domination-_the_jewish_revolt_and_the_destruction_of_the_second_temple-_part_ii/
source2: Richard Gottheil and Isaac Broyde, 'Hyrcanus II', Jewish Encyclopedia, 1906 - https://jewishencyclopedia.com/articles/7973-hyrcanus-ii
notes: Pompey took the Temple in 63 BCE; Hyrcanus II reappointed high priest without political authority. Roman ruling elite kept Roman religion; Christianity (a third tradition) came only in the 4th century.

source2: Metropolitan Museum of Art, folio from a Harivamsa made for Akbar, ca. 1590-95, collection object page - https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/448183
notes: Mughals remained Muslim, but Akbar's court patronized Hindu tradition: Hindu epics translated into Persian (established by 1574, Met), Hindu theologians in court debates (Met essay), and Din-i Ilahi borrowing Hindu elements (Britannica). Patronage, not conversion.

Ghur Islamized through 11th-century Ghaznavid raids; Ghurids Sunni. In 612/1215 Khwarazmshah Ala al-Din Muhammad deposed the last Firuzkuh sultan (Iranica). Khwarazmshahs: Muslim Turkish dynasty descended from a Seljuq governor, with literate Persianate court.

source1: Svat Soucek, 'The Shaybanids', ch. 11 in A History of Inner Asia, Cambridge University Press, 2000 - https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs/history-of-inner-asia/shaybanids/681328EFAC754EF2B9D3E7CF4BFE8CB7
source2: N. D. Sultanbayeva and Z. Shadkam, 'The Role of Mukhammad Shaybani Khan's Works within the Classical Chaghatay Literature', Bulletin of L.N. Gumilyov Eurasian National University 155(2), 2026 - https://bulpolit.enu.kz/index.php/main/article/view/997
notes: Shaybani seized Samarkand c. 1500-01 and Herat 1507; Soucek: Uzbeks and Timurids 'both were Sunni Muslims', with cultural continuity. Shaybani wrote a Chagatay Divan and a fiqh treatise affirming Sunni Islam.

source2: Christopher Harrison, France and Islam in West Africa, 1860-1960, Cambridge University Press, 1988, chapter 'French Islamic policy in crisis: the Futa Jallon 1909-1912' (online text) - https://webpulaaku.site/defte/harrison_christopher/french_islamic_policy.html
notes: Futa Jallon was a Muslim theocratic state; French troops occupied Timbo in 1896. French rulers (Catholic heritage, secular-republican officials) surveilled and co-opted Muslim chiefs, seeking to 'channel' Islam (Harrison), but never adopted it.

Macedonian officer Seleucus I killed Lysimachus at Corupedium, 281 BCE, then died near Lysimachia (killed by Ptolemy Keraunos, also Macedonian). Conquerors and conquered shared Greco-Macedonian religion and Greek writing.

Galdan was educated in Tibet as a Buddhist lama (Dzungars adopted Buddhism in 17th century); Khalkha led by Zanabazar, enthroned 1640 as incarnate lama. Both Tibetan Buddhist; Mongol script used for Buddhist texts. Qing crushed Galdan 1696.
